reviews.review: Very cool and interesting hacker game. The hacking part is lightweight (it is a game afterall), but you never feel tedious in typing those commands.

As a Kali Linux user, I can assure you that this game is almost 100% accurate when it comes about the commands. I say "almost" because some features like "PortHack" do not exist in real coding ( I think ). This game is perfect in introducing you into a "hacking" world, which you will love if you are into this stuff. I recommend this game with all my heart, give it a shot, see if you can enjoy it at least as I did. The only negative side of this game is that at some point you may think it becomes repetitive, and you'd be right, but the hacking atmosphere will make you to want to continue. I rate this game 10/10 and would like to see more updates and more levels.

There are also many easter eggs in the game. Soundtrack is hype. Generally I will give this game a 9/10. I will no doubt buy the next DLC of this game.

[h1]Never played something like this. Now I am a text-game nerd. Ty, Hacknet. [/h1]

Hacknet was my first text based game. Ever. It took me 6 hours to finish. Although I got it in a sale for around 3€, I would definitely pay the full price for it.

I cannot tell anything different but that I really enjoyed this game. Even though I highly dislike working with Unix-like shells, Hacknet keeps it simple enough to not completely mess everything up (as I expected it to be). Sure, you have to use the "help" command here and there, but that's what makes the game.

The puzzles are pretty challenging from time to time, which may (or may not) extend the game to 8, maybe 10 hours. Also messing with other people's private files is pretty entertaining, since the developers included some bash.org stuff.

The only negative aspect about Hacknet is the routine of doing some things over and over again. But compared to "real" hacking, this is still acceptable.

9/10. Would buy this again.

Hacknet is exactly what it sounds like:  It's a game where you hack computers, get some info, maybe some new software, and repeat.  You do this with the main objective of uncovering what happened to a hacker named Bit (1 or 0 I wonder).  As the story progresses, hacking becomes much more difficult due to higher levels of security and of course forgetting where the computer that you need to hack is on the net map (it is very cluttered by the end of the game).

The game does a fairly good job of making you care about the story in the beginning, the part where Bit is actually guiding you and talking to you, and then kind of forgets about it until the very end.  Don't be deceived though:  Everything you do in the main part of the game is absolutely necessary in order to complete the game.  You learn new tricks, get new software, and discover more organizations linked to Bit in some way or another.  It isn't the most compelling story, but the gameplay and story are very much intertwined.

Speaking of, the actual game itself is very engaging.  No cutscenes, no voice overs (save for one), no fancy bloom effects or explosions.  Just you and your computer.  You can watch the trailer on the game's store page to get a feel for what it looks like.  You get four different screens:  a RAM screen where you can see which programs/notes are actively running, a net map showing active nodes that you can connect to, a GUI, and a terminal.  The terminal is a nice touch and is very UNIX like, if you like that sort of thing.  However, I resorted to the GUI more often than not when I was on the clock due to a trace program, but having both options is a must when you need to copy some files or the like since the GUI is limited in what it can do.

Hacking becomes second nature after doing it a few times, and it runs the risk of becoming a bit too repetitive at some points.  Generally, there are four ports (five or six for computers later in the game) and sometimes a proxy, firewall, or both.  You can hack multiple ports at once, and sometimes it is required, but keep an eye on the RAM screen.  Run out of memory and your hack will take longer.  Once done, enjoy the files on that computer.  Sometimes there are new programs to download and there are almost always files in the home folder to give you some laughs.

You can beat the game in under 10 hours once you get the hang of it.  That would not appeal to most people, but there is so many files in the game that you can go through and quite a few programs that you can probably get another 10 hours out of it.  Add that to the number of computers in the game that you have access to and that's probably another 3 hours or so.  I am actually playing through it again because I missed out on some computers from my last playthrough.  "Highly addicting" is the best way to describe it.

Whether you're into computers or not, you should give this game a go.  Also, type "openCDtray" once you are in the game.  You'll thank me later.

I didn't enjoy this game much at all. I like the idea of playing a hacking simulator, but the execution really fell flat. The challenges are monotonous and uninteresting. The files added in for flavor are tired-old jokes. There's not much in the way of story. And the interface is awful. The worst part is the network map where you connect to hosts, which is a crowded bunch of unlabeled dots that you just have to remember, (I eventually gave up and put the list of hosts/IPs into a text document on a second monitor so that I could at least hide the ones I thought I was done with) but the terminal and RAM screens are both pretty bad too. The RAM screen is a combination of an arbitrary hurdle and an excuse to add silly hacker media trope animations, and I want to know what program spends 300MB of ram displaying a short text file. The terminal doesn't scroll or even have history, so once some output goes off the top of the screen it's lost. Did you cat a file and not bother to read it until after rm /log/*; dc;? Have fun breaking back in to get the file again since a bunch of "Deleting file" messages pushed it off the screen? Did you want to !solve because you didn't get everything you wanted the first time you broke in? Too bad.

Definitely not worth the price or your time.

Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

This is not a game I hate. However, much like that TIS-100 game, I was left completely clueless as to how to proceed, though nowhere near as quickly, thanks to an actual tutorial and being able to play a little bit of the game before getting stuck, as well as a help menu listing commands. As a child in the 80s, I spent a fair amount of time using DOS to find files, modify them, etc., and in college, I used UNIX for a semester, scoring an A. There isn't a day that goes by where I don't use a PC, unless something really weird happens, like a blackout. Therefore, I was more than a little surprised when I got so hopelessly dumbfounded by this game. Granted, this game is far classier than TIS-100.

This game actually has music, and it's quite nice, while TIS-100 had none that I found. TIS-100's manual was difficult to understand and quite daunting, while Hacknet is far more user friendly, and really appears to have a story and more purpose to it. That said, the game left me confused and stuck when I came upon a firewall. The game never covered how to deal with firewalls in the tutorial. I tried running a program I had just downloaded from another computer in-game, which let me access one port, but I couldn't access any of the other ports. I used every page of help to look up commands that could help me, and analyzing the firewall brought up a wall of letters and numbers that didn't seem to do anything, and selecting to "solve" the firewall didn't do anything, either. I checked every computer I had access to and found nothing else that could help me.

If I'm stuck this early in, checking a walkthrough or asking for help online will likely lead to me continuing my confused wandering without learning anything within the game itself. I should not have to rely on the Internet to learn how to play a game for fun...

I'm disappointed in the game, but only because I liked what I saw when the game was presenting things in a way that cleverly educates the player, but then it throws you a problem early-game that no amount of searching within the game itself appears to turn up a solution. The point where it figuratively drops you in the deep end of the digital pool with a cyber-anchor tied to your feet is where I lose any ability to appreciate the game beyond that point.

It's also entirely possible I lack the mental faculties to interact with this digital gaming experience in a fulfilling manner. If that's the case, then so be it, but I must represent the "mentally deficient" population and state that I do not recommend this game as a result.

I am seriously digging this game. I got it from the Dec 2016 monthly Humble Bundle. It makes me feel more like a real hacker than real hacking probably would. :P

Seriously though, you get the thrill of breaking into secure computers and digging around finding secrets and reading files -- but without, you know, actually needing to spend years learning how to do it and without actually committing felonies.

It's exciting joining secret hacking groups and being assigned missions. There's a sense of panic when another hacker starts counter-hacking you and messing with your system.

The main issue with this game is also its biggest strength -- and that is that it really is a computer terminal simulator. There are some fancy graphics to make hacking seem a bit more exciting, but ultimately it really is just entering commands in a command prompt and anwering emails. This is what makes it "feel" like real hacking, which is what makes it fun and special to me. But I'm sure some people will be turned off by the fact that the game is mostly reading and typing -- basically a hacking-themed, text-based adventure. Like Zork -- except instead of "enter room" "take scroll" it's "connect 205.34.1.220" "scp scroll.txt". Which, when you think about it, is kinda the same thing. :P

I'm recommending this because I'm having a blast, but just make sure it's the sort of thing you would enjoy before buying it.

This game was a great idea with very poor followthrough. You learn two or three tricks to bypass security, have to collect the appropriate scripts to defeat each of the half dozen interfaces, and then boom, you're a legendary hacker. It seemed like there were alot of mechanics that they planned, but never got around to implementing. All that hype about deleting the logs after you access a computer... maybe I missed something, but I couldn't see that it did anything. And the Trap and Forkbombs... were those actually useful somehow? Oh, and it was very easy to make game-breaking mistakes, like deleting a file you were supposed to steal. Alot of silent ways to ruin the game and be unable to recover... hope you didn't save after one of those.

A great hollywood-hacking game, comparable to Uplink in a number of ways. The game encourages more command-line interaction, and it works well. Though where Uplink is mostly random missions, Hacknet has each mission written separately. The writing and "level" design are very good, even for the unimportant random missions. I played through the game a second time to see the missions that I missed on my first playthrough. The presentation is great, and the music definitely sets the mood. Worth full price.

Terminal-based hacking sim with optional GUI. If you are familiar with using bash and the GNU userland in the real world, you will notice some edge cases (particularly with cd) that are valid commands in bash, but won't work in-game. It doesn't detract too much from the game overall, though - it's still a high quality emulation of the traditional unix environment.

The plot is a little predictable but is still interesting. There are a few interesting subplots, and I was pleasantly surprised at how deeply the world is fleshed out. You can even hack into the in-game mail server and read other people's messages.

Note that if you are on an optimus laptop, the game defaults to running on the integrated GPU, which can cause it to chug if you have all of the graphical effects on.
